Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $k$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+k[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ k[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ k[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get 

$$
3k=-6\,⟹\,k=-2.
$$

But then

$$
\begin{aligned}-2[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\ne [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $k$ such that $3{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2}=0.$
